summary: Specifies how to protect the Babel routing protocol with Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS). Babel has no built-in way to authenticate neighbours or protect messages, and this adds authentication, integrity, and confidentiality between neighbouring routers.

plainLanguage.summary: This puts Babel's messages inside a locked, tamper-proof envelope so only trusted neighbours can read and send them.

who is the dtls client in babel
subtitle: How Babel routers use DTLS to authenticate neighbours and keep their routing messages private and tamper-proof.

tldr.problem: The Babel routing protocol has no way to authenticate neighbours or protect messages, so an attacker can send crafted messages that pull traffic toward the attacker or an under-resourced target.
tldr.mechanism: Babel nodes run DTLS on a separate UDP port (6699). The node with the lower address is the DTLS client, all unicast Babel traffic is protected, and only plain Multicast Hellos are sent in the clear.
tldr.outcome: Neighbours get mutual authentication, integrity, replay protection and confidentiality. It gives a single authentication domain, so any node with the right credentials can convey any routing information.

today: RFC 8968 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the defined way to protect Babel with DTLS; the alternative is Babel-MAC in RFC 8967.

sections.title: Why Babel Needs Protection
sections.content:
The Babel routing protocol (RFC 8966) does not contain any means to authenticate neighbours or protect the messages sent between them. An attacker can therefore send maliciously crafted Babel messages that lead a network to route traffic to the attacker or to an under-resourced target, causing denial of service.

This document uses Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS, RFC 6347) to prevent such attacks. It inherits what DTLS offers: authentication, integrity, optional replay protection, confidentiality and asymmetric keying.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now anyone can shout fake directions at a router and it will believe them. DTLS makes routers check who is talking first.

sections.title: Applicability and Alternatives
sections.content:
Another way to secure Babel exists: MAC authentication, called Babel-MAC (RFC 8967). It only offers basic features, namely authentication, integrity and replay protection with a small number of symmetric keys. Babel over DTLS is expected to suit a wider range of environments.

Babel over DTLS provides a single authentication domain: every node that has the right credentials can convey any and all routing information. DTLS supports several ways for nodes to identify themselves. This document does not say which to use; identity management is left to deployment profiles.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone with the right key card can walk in and say anything about the roads. The RFC does not pick the kind of key card; that is up to each network.

sections.title: Starting a DTLS Connection
sections.content:
DTLS is client-server, but Babel is peer-to-peer, and DTLS only protects unicast while Babel also uses multicast. To bridge this, every node MUST act as a DTLS server on one UDP port and MUST listen for unprotected Babel on a different one. The DTLS port is registered as babel-dtls (UDP port 6699); plain Babel uses the babel port (UDP port 6696).

When a node discovers a neighbour, usually from an unprotected multicast packet, it compares the neighbour's IP address with its own in network byte order. The node with the lowest address acts as the DTLS client. The client connects from an ephemeral UDP port, and SHOULD use a different ephemeral port from recently used connections so servers can tell old and new connections apart. DTLS connection identifiers are an alternative.

A receiving node MUST check that the source is an IPv6 link-local address or an IPv4 address on the local network, and reject the connection otherwise. Authentication is mutual: clients MUST authenticate servers and servers MUST authenticate clients, and implementations MUST support checking peers against a local store of credentials. Nodes MUST only negotiate DTLS version 1.2 or higher, MUST follow BCP 195 and MUST use DTLS replay protection. If a new connection arrives from a neighbour that already has one, the older connection MUST NOT be dropped until the new handshake has completed and the peer's identity is validated.
sections.plainLanguage: Two neighbours decide who knocks on whose door by comparing addresses: the lower one knocks. Both must show ID before they talk.

sections.title: What Is Sent Protected and What Is Not
sections.content:
The whole Babel packet, from the Magic byte of the header to the last byte of the trailer, is sent inside DTLS. Nodes MUST NOT send any TLVs over the unprotected port except Hello TLVs without the Unicast flag set, and MUST NOT send unprotected unicast packets. Unless another discovery mechanism exists, nodes SHOULD periodically send unprotected Multicast Hellos to find new neighbours. To track two-way reachability they can rely on those Multicast Hellos or add protected Unicast Hellos.

On reception, nodes MUST silently ignore any unprotected unicast packet, all non-Hello TLVs in unprotected packets, and any unprotected Hello with the Unicast flag set. An ignored packet can still reveal a new neighbour.

An implementation can be built from plain Babel by replacing each multicast TLV with a separate unicast TLV for every neighbour. Nodes SHOULD tie DTLS state to the neighbour table entry, and when the entry is flushed they SHOULD discard the state and, if the link still seems viable, send a DTLS close_notify alert.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a short "I am here" shout goes out in the open. Everything about the roads is whispered privately to each neighbour, and anything else shouted in the open is ignored.

sections.title: Mixing With Unprotected Babel
sections.content:
A node MAY support both Babel over DTLS and unprotected Babel, and MAY run both at once, but MUST do so on separate interfaces, because the security of Babel over DTLS depends on ignoring unprotected packets other than Multicast Hellos. An implementation may allow unprotected Babel on some interfaces, which gives nodes there the same access as authenticated nodes. This SHOULD NOT be done unless the interface authenticates nodes at a lower layer, such as IPsec.

If both kinds of Babel share a network, DTLS nodes will see unprotected Multicast Hellos and try to start DTLS connections, which nodes running only unprotected Babel will not answer. Implementations SHOULD therefore rate-limit connection attempts.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can speak both the secret and the open language, but never on the same street, or the open language could sneak past the guard.

sections.title: Packet Size and Handshake Cost
sections.content:
DTLS adds a header, an authentication tag and possibly padding to every packet, which shrinks the Babel payload. The packet size rules of RFC 8966 are not relaxed, but nodes SHOULD compute the DTLS overhead for their ciphersuites and SHOULD NOT send Babel packets larger than the interface MTU minus IP, UDP and DTLS overhead. Different connections may use different ciphers, so the MTU to one neighbour can differ from another on the same link.

Receivers MUST accept packets as large as the interface MTU adjusted for UDP and IP headers, or 512 octets, whichever is larger. This does not count DTLS overhead, because the peer may not be able to compute it.

Appendix A suggests ways to cut handshake size: raw public keys (RFC 7250), the Cached Information Extension (RFC 7924) to avoid resending a certificate that can be several kilobytes, and TLS False Start (RFC 7918) to save round trips.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret envelope takes up room, so each note has to be a bit shorter to fit in the mailbox.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious client may start many DTLS handshakes, possibly keeping them open as long as it can (the Slowloris style of attack), and IPv6 temporary addresses make clients hard to identify before the handshake ends. Servers need mitigation such as limiting handshake rates from a subnet.

Because Multicast Hellos are unprotected, attackers can tamper with them, for example with wrong Seqno and Interval values that break bidirectional reachability detection. Implementations MAY use Multicast Hellos for link quality estimation but SHOULD also send protected Unicast Hellos.

DTLS cannot detect an active on-path attacker who captures valid packets and resends them later, which could make a node think a departed neighbour is still reachable. Nodes MUST discard the DTLS state for a neighbour after a finite time without valid DTLS packets, for example when its IHU timer fires. Hellos alone are not enough since Multicast Hellos are unprotected. Dropping packets reordered by more than two IHU intervals limits the spread of stale routing information.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard can be tired out by lots of fake visitors, and a thief can replay an old recording. So the guard limits visitors and forgets neighbours who have gone quiet.
